items.prompt: Santi is walking through a garden and suddenly smells a very sweet scent coming from a nearby flower. Which sense organ is Santi using to detect this scent?
items.helper_text: Think about which body part you use when you breathe in an aroma.

options.label: A
options.text: Eyes

options.label: B
options.text: Ears

options.label: C
options.text: Nose

options.label: D
options.text: Tongue

items.explanation: The sense of smell is processed by the nose. When Santi detects a scent, the chemical particles in the air enter her nostrils and are detected by her nose.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the nose as the organ for smelling.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the tongue (taste) with the nose (smell).
Thinking all senses work together simultaneously for a single stimulus.

items.prompt: Budi has been playing football in the bright sunlight for two hours without wearing a hat or sunglasses. He now feels a stinging sensation in his eyes. What is the best way for Budi to protect his eyes in the future?
items.helper_text: Look for a solution that provides a protective shield for the eyes.

options.label: A
options.text: Rubbing his eyes with dirty hands

options.label: B
options.text: Wearing sunglasses when playing outside

options.label: C
options.text: Closing his eyes all day

options.label: D
options.text: Looking directly at the sun to see better

items.explanation: Sunglasses act as a protective barrier that filters out harmful UV rays from the sun, preventing eye irritation and damage caused by bright light.

rubric.correct: The student selects a preventative health measure to protect the eyes from light.
common_misconceptions: Choosing a temporary fix (like closing eyes) instead of a preventative habit.
Choosing actions that could cause more harm (like rubbing eyes).

items.prompt: Rani is eating a bowl of hot soup. She notices that the soup is very hot and tastes very salty. Which two senses is Rani using at the same time to experience her meal?
items.helper_text: Identify which sense detects 'temperature' and which sense detects 'flavor'.

options.label: A
options.text: Sight and Hearing

options.label: B
options.text: Touch and Smell

options.label: C
options.text: Touch and Taste

options.label: D
options.text: Hearing and Taste

items.explanation: Feeling the temperature (hot) is a sensation of touch (detected by the skin/mouth), and recognizing the saltiness is a sensation of taste (detected by the tongue).

rubric.correct: The student correctly connects temperature to touch and flavor to taste.
common_misconceptions: Assuming 'hot' is only related to smell.
Confusing the sense of taste with the sense of smell.

items.prompt: Siti is walking through a garden. She sees a bright red flower, smells a sweet fragrance, and feels the soft texture of the petals. Which sequence of senses did Siti use in the correct order based on the description?
items.helper_text: Match the sensory organ to the action described in the story.

options.label: A
options.text: Touch $\rightarrow$ Sight $\rightarrow$ Smell

options.label: B
options.text: Sight $\rightarrow$ Smell $\rightarrow$ Touch

options.label: C
options.text: Smell $\rightarrow$ Sight $\rightarrow$ Touch

options.label: D
options.text: Sight $\rightarrow$ Touch $\rightarrow$ Smell

items.explanation: Siti first sees the color (sight), then smells the fragrance (smell), and finally feels the texture (touch).

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the chronological sequence of sensory inputs.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the order of events described in the text.
Mixing up which sense is used for color versus texture.

items.prompt: If a person is wearing thick earmuffs that completely cover their ears, which of the following scenarios is most likely to happen?
items.helper_text: Think about which body part is being covered by the earmuffs.

options.label: A
options.text: They will be able to see colors more clearly.

options.label: B
options.text: They will struggle to hear someone calling their name.

options.label: C
options.text: They will lose their sense of balance immediately.

options.label: D
options.text: They will be unable to taste their food.

items.explanation: Earmuffs block sound waves from entering the ear canal, which directly impacts the sense of hearing.

rubric.correct: The student connects the physical barrier to the impairment of the specific sense.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that blocking one sense affects an unrelated sense like sight.
Confusing hearing with the vestibular system (balance) in a way that implies immediate loss.

items.prompt: Budi has a very sore throat and a high fever. He finds it difficult to swallow and feels very weak. Based on these symptoms, what is the most logical advice for Budi's health?
items.helper_text: Consider what the body needs most when it is fighting an illness.

options.label: A
options.text: He should run a marathon to sweat out the fever.

options.label: B
options.text: He should eat very spicy food to kill the germs.

options.label: C
options.text: He should rest and drink plenty of water.

options.label: D
options.text: He should avoid sleeping so the fever goes away faster.

items.explanation: Rest allows the body to use energy to fight infection, and water prevents dehydration caused by fever.

rubric.correct: The student selects the most medically sound recovery method for a fever and sore throat.
common_misconceptions: Choosing high-activity options that would actually exhaust a sick person.
Believing that irritating the throat with spicy food helps a sore throat.

items.prompt: Why is it important to wash our hands with soap before eating, rather than just using plain water?
items.helper_text: Think about what 'germs' are and why they stick to our skin.

options.label: A
options.text: Soap makes the hands smell better than water does.

options.label: B
options.text: Water alone cannot effectively remove oils and microscopic germs.

options.label: C
options.text: Soap helps the food taste much better when we eat it.

options.label: D
options.text: Water is too cold and can make our stomachs hurt.

items.explanation: Soap is a surfactant that breaks down oils and lifts germs away from the skin, which plain water cannot do effectively.

rubric.correct: The student understands the functional difference between cleaning with soap and water regarding hygiene.
common_misconceptions: Focusing on the scent or taste rather than the hygiene aspect.
Thinking water is useless, rather than understanding it is just less effective than soap.

items.prompt: A chef is cooking in a kitchen. He accidentally touches a very hot pan. Which sequence of events describes how his body responds?
items.helper_text: Follow the path of information: Stimulus $\rightarrow$ Sense Organ $\rightarrow$ Brain $\rightarrow$ Action.

options.label: A
options.text: The pan sees the hand $\rightarrow$ sends a signal to the brain $\rightarrow$ the hand moves.

options.label: B
options.text: The skin feels heat $\rightarrow$ sends a signal to the brain $\rightarrow$ the brain tells the muscles to move.

options.label: C
options.text: The brain feels heat $\rightarrow$ tells the skin to move $\rightarrow$ the pan gets cold.

options.label: D
options.text: The muscles feel heat $\rightarrow$ tell the skin to jump $\rightarrow$ the brain watches.

items.explanation: The sensory organ (skin) detects the stimulus, sends a signal through the nervous system to the brain, which then processes the information and sends a command to the muscles.

rubric.correct: The student correctly sequences the biological response to a stimulus.
common_misconceptions: Placing the brain as the initial detector of the heat.
Reversing the order of the signal (thinking the brain detects first).

items.prompt: If a person's sense of smell is blocked due to a very bad cold, how will this most likely affect their sense of taste?
items.helper_text: Think about what happens when you hold your nose while eating an onion.

options.label: A
options.text: Their sense of taste will become much stronger.

options.label: B
options.text: Their sense of taste will be completely destroyed forever.

options.label: C
options.text: They will find it difficult to identify flavors in food.

options.label: D
options.text: The taste will change to being only salty.

items.explanation: Flavor is a combination of taste (tongue) and smell (nose). When smell is blocked, the brain cannot fully perceive the complexity of flavors.

rubric.correct: The student recognizes the interconnection between the sense of smell and the perception of flavor.
common_misconceptions: Thinking taste and smell are completely independent processes.
Thinking the tongue itself stops working.

items.prompt: Which of these daily habits provides the BEST long-term protection for both the eyes and the skeletal system?
items.helper_text: Look for a choice that addresses both eyes and bones.

options.label: A
options.text: Eating lots of sugary candy every day.

options.label: B
options.text: Sitting in a dark room to rest your eyes.

options.label: C
options.text: Eating vegetables rich in Vitamin A and drinking milk for calcium.

options.label: D
options.text: Wearing sunglasses only when it is raining.

items.explanation: Vitamin A is essential for eye health, and calcium is crucial for maintaining strong bones (the skeletal system).

rubric.correct: The student links specific nutrients to the health of two different body systems.
common_misconceptions: Selecting an option that only helps one system.
Choosing a habit that is actually harmful (like too much sugar).

items.prompt: A farmer notices that his tomato plants are wilting and looking very thirsty, even though he waters the soil every day. He discovers that the plant's roots are damaged by insects. Why are the plants wilting?
items.helper_text: Think about which part of the plant acts like a straw to drink water from the ground.

options.label: A
options.text: The leaves cannot catch enough sunlight to make food.

options.label: B
options.text: The roots cannot absorb water from the soil to send to the rest of the plant.

options.label: C
options.text: The stem is too weak to hold the plant upright.

options.label: D
options.text: The flowers are falling off because of the insects.

items.explanation: Roots are responsible for absorbing water and nutrients from the soil. If the roots are damaged, the plant cannot take in the water it needs to stay hydrated, causing it to wilt even if the soil is wet.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the root's role in water absorption.
common_misconceptions: Thinking that wilting is only caused by a lack of sunlight.
Confusing the function of the stem (support) with the function of the roots (absorption).

items.prompt: Siti is conducting an experiment. She covers all the leaves of a small plant with dark, thick cloth for one week. What is the most likely result of this experiment?
items.helper_text: Remember what leaves need from the sun to make food for the plant.

options.label: A
options.text: The plant will grow taller because it is protected from the wind.

options.label: B
options.text: The plant will produce more flowers because it is resting.

options.label: C
options.text: The plant will become weak and unhealthy because it cannot make food.

options.label: D
options.text: The plant will absorb more water through its leaves.

items.explanation: Leaves are the part of the plant where photosynthesis occurs. Photosynthesis requires sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into food (glucose). By covering the leaves, the plant cannot access sunlight and will fail to produce the food it needs to survive.

rubric.correct: The student correctly relates sunlight access via leaves to the plant's ability to produce food.
common_misconceptions: Believing that leaves are only for breathing and do not make food.
Assuming plants can make food using only water without sunlight.

items.prompt: A farmer notices that his tomato plants are wilting even though the soil is very wet. Upon inspection, he finds that the roots are turning black and mushy. What is the most likely reason the plants are wilting?
items.helper_text: Think about what part of the plant is responsible for taking in water from the ground.

options.label: A
options.text: The leaves are unable to capture sunlight for photosynthesis.

options.label: B
options.text: The damaged roots can no longer absorb water and nutrients from the soil.

options.label: C
options.text: The stems are too weak to hold the weight of the heavy fruit.

options.label: D
options.text: The flowers are unable to produce seeds to keep the plant alive.

items.explanation: Wilting occurs when a plant lacks water pressure. If the roots are damaged (rotting due to too much water), they cannot perform their primary function of absorbing water, leading to dehydration despite the wet soil.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies that root damage prevents water absorption.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the plant is wilting because it has too much water.
Confusing the function of leaves with the function of roots.

items.prompt: If a scientist covers all the leaves of a healthy plant with thick, opaque black plastic, what will most likely happen to the plant after several days?
items.helper_text: What is the main job of a leaf in terms of making food?

options.label: A
options.text: The plant will grow faster because it is protected from insects.

options.label: B
options.text: The plant will produce more flowers to find more light.

options.label: C
options.text: The plant will weaken and die because it cannot make food.

options.label: D
options.text: The plant will grow longer roots to find more nutrients.

items.explanation: Leaves are the site of photosynthesis. Without light, the plant cannot convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose (food), leading to starvation.

rubric.correct: The student understands that leaves need light to produce food via photosynthesis.
common_misconceptions: Believing plants only need water and soil to survive.
Thinking leaves are only for breathing and not for food production.

items.prompt: A plant has a very thick, woody stem. Compared to a plant with a soft, green stem, what is the most likely advantage of this woody stem?
items.helper_text: Consider how a strong structure helps a plant reach for the sun.

options.label: A
options.text: It helps the plant absorb more sunlight.

options.label: B
options.text: It allows the plant to grow taller and support more weight.

options.label: C
options.text: It helps the plant attract more pollinators like bees.

options.label: D
options.text: It allows the plant to breathe more easily.

items.explanation: The stem's function is to support the plant and transport nutrients. A woody, thick stem provides structural strength, allowing the plant to grow tall and carry heavy branches or fruit.

rubric.correct: The student links stem thickness to structural support and height.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the stem's thickness is only for storing water.
Confusing stem support with leaf surface area.

items.prompt: In a desert, many plants have very long roots that spread out wide just below the surface. Why is this an important adaptation?
items.helper_text: How can a plant catch water before it disappears into the dry sand?

options.label: A
options.text: To help the plant stay anchored during heavy sandstorms.

options.label: B
options.text: To allow the plant to breathe in the dry air.

options.label: C
options.text: To quickly absorb as much water as possible from rare rainfall.

options.label: D
options.text: To protect the plant from being eaten by animals.

items.explanation: In deserts, rain is infrequent and often evaporates quickly. Wide, shallow roots allow the plant to capture moisture from the surface immediately when it rains.

rubric.correct: The student relates root structure to the specific environmental need for water collection.
common_misconceptions: Focusing only on stability (anchoring) rather than nutrient/water absorption.
Thinking roots are used for protection from animals.

items.prompt: A researcher applies a chemical to a plant that specifically blocks the 'stomata' (tiny holes) on the leaves. What will be the most immediate effect on the plant?
items.helper_text: Think about how a plant 'breathes' through its leaves.

options.label: A
options.text: The plant will stop absorbing water from the roots.

options.label: B
options.text: The plant will be unable to exchange gases like carbon dioxide.

options.label: C
options.text: The plant will grow much larger leaves to compensate.

options.label: D
options.text: The plant will produce more sugar in its stem.

items.explanation: Stomata are small openings on leaves used for gas exchange (taking in CO2 and releasing Oxygen). If they are blocked, the plant cannot get the CO2 needed for photosynthesis.

rubric.correct: The student identifies the role of stomata in gas exchange.
common_misconceptions: Thinking stomata are used for absorbing water.
Thinking stomata are part of the root system.

items.prompt: If you were to move a plant from a dark room to a bright sunny window, you might notice it starts growing toward the light. Which part of the plant is 'detecting' the light and moving the plant?
items.helper_text: Which parts of the plant are directly exposed to the sun and responsible for making food?

options.label: A
options.text: The roots, because they feel the warmth of the sun.

options.label: B
options.text: The flowers, because they want to attract insects.

options.label: C
options.text: The stem and leaves, to maximize light capture.

options.label: D
options.text: The seeds, because they contain the instructions for growth.

items.explanation: The stem and leaves are the primary parts interacting with light. The stem grows toward the light (phototropism) to position the leaves optimally for photosynthesis.

rubric.correct: The student identifies the stem/leaves as the parts responsible for light interaction.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the roots move the plant toward the light.
Believing the movement is caused by the flowers.

items.prompt: A plant has very large, wide leaves. In which type of environment would this plant most likely thrive?
items.helper_text: Large leaves are like big solar panels. When would a plant need a 'big solar panel'?

options.label: A
options.text: A very hot, dry desert with little sunlight.

options.label: B
options.text: A dark forest floor where sunlight is scarce.

options.label: C
options.text: A windy mountain top with constant moving air.

options.label: D
options.text: A place with extremely high salt levels in the soil.

items.explanation: Large leaves provide a bigger surface area to capture as much sunlight as possible. This is an advantage in shady environments (like a forest floor) where light is limited.

rubric.correct: The student connects leaf surface area to the need for light absorption in low-light areas.
common_misconceptions: Thinking large leaves are good for dry deserts (where they would actually lose too much water).
Thinking large leaves help with wind resistance.

items.concept_title: Human body parts and the senses
items.prompt: Budi is walking in a garden and suddenly hears a loud buzzing sound near his ear. Which sense organ is Budi using to detect this sound?
items.helper_text: Think about which part of your body you use to hear things.

options.label: A
options.text: Nose

options.label: B
options.text: Eyes

options.label: C
options.text: Ears

options.label: D
options.text: Tongue

items.explanation: Sound is a vibration that is detected by the ears. When Budi hears the buzzing, his ears are the sense organs processing the auditory information.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the ear as the organ for hearing.
common_misconceptions: Confusing hearing with sight (eyes) because the bee might be visible.
Thinking the nose is involved because of the smell of flowers.

items.concept_title: Human body parts and the senses
items.prompt: Siti is eating a slice of lemon. She makes a funny face because the taste is very sour. Which sense organ is primarily responsible for identifying the sour taste?
items.helper_text: Which body part do you use when you are tasting food?

options.label: A
options.text: Skin

options.label: B
options.text: Tongue

options.label: C
options.text: Nose

options.label: D
options.text: Eyes

items.explanation: The tongue is covered in taste buds that allow us to distinguish between sweet, sour, salty, and bitter flavors. The sourness of the lemon is detected by the tongue.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the tongue as the organ for taste.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the nose is the primary organ (though smell affects flavor, the direct detection of 'sour' is taste).
Confusing taste with touch (skin).

items.concept_title: Human body parts and the senses
items.prompt: Rina is walking in a garden and suddenly smells something very sweet, but she cannot see where it is coming from. Which sequence of events correctly describes how her body processes this information?
items.helper_text: Think about the order: Stimulus $\rightarrow$ Sense Organ $\rightarrow$ Nerve $\rightarrow$ Brain.

options.label: A
options.text: Scent particles enter the nose $\rightarrow$ nerves send signals to the brain $\rightarrow$ the brain identifies the smell.

options.label: B
options.text: The brain sends a signal to the nose $\rightarrow$ scent particles enter $\rightarrow$ the nose identifies the smell.

options.label: C
options.text: Scent particles enter the nose $\rightarrow$ the nose sends signals to the eyes $\rightarrow$ the eyes identify the smell.

options.label: D
options.text: The eyes see the scent $\rightarrow$ the nose smells the scent $\rightarrow$ the brain processes the scent.

items.explanation: Sensation begins when a stimulus (scent) hits the organ (nose), which then uses nerves to transmit information to the brain for interpretation.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the sensory pathway starting from the stimulus to the brain.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the nose itself 'thinks' or identifies the smell.
Thinking the brain sends the signal to the nose to start the smelling process.

items.concept_title: Human body parts and the senses
items.prompt: If a person is wearing thick earplugs that block all sound, which of the following sensory experiences would be most affected, and why?
items.helper_text: Does the ear only help us hear, or does it have another hidden job?

options.label: A
options.text: Sight, because the ears and eyes work together to see clearly.

options.label: B
options.text: Balance, because the inner ear is responsible for maintaining stability.

options.label: C
options.text: Touch, because sound vibrations are felt through the skin.

options.label: D
options.text: Smell, because sound waves carry scent particles into the nose.

items.explanation: While earplugs block hearing (auditory), the inner ear is also the organ responsible for the sense of balance (vestibular system). Blocking the ear can disrupt this complex system.

rubric.correct: The student connects the ear anatomy to the function of balance beyond just hearing.
common_misconceptions: Assuming the ear is only for hearing.
Believing that blocking sound has no effect on other body functions.

items.concept_title: Human body parts and the senses
items.prompt: A chef is cooking soup. He accidentally adds too much salt. Even though he is wearing a mask that covers his nose, he can still tell something is wrong when he tastes the soup. Why does the sense of taste change when the nose is blocked?
items.helper_text: Consider how flavor is different from just basic tastes like salty or sweet.

options.label: A
options.text: The tongue can only taste salt, but not flavor.

options.label: B
options.text: Taste and smell work together to create the perception of flavor.

options.label: C
options.text: The salt travels from the tongue directly to the ears.

options.label: D
options.text: The mask makes the tongue more sensitive to salt.

items.explanation: Flavor is a combination of taste (from the tongue) and smell (from the nose). While the 'flavor' might be duller without smell, the tongue can still detect the chemical sensation of salt.

rubric.correct: The student understands the synergy between the olfactory and gustatory systems.
common_misconceptions: Thinking taste and smell are the exact same thing.
Thinking the tongue cannot taste anything if the nose is blocked.

items.concept_title: Human body parts and the senses
items.prompt: A student is playing a game in a dark room. They can feel the texture of a ball (rough or smooth) and its temperature (hot or cold), but they cannot see it. Which sensory organs are working together to provide this information?
items.helper_text: Focus on which part of the body feels texture and temperature.

options.label: A
options.text: The eyes and the skin.

options.label: B
options.text: The skin and the ears.

options.label: C
options.text: The skin and the nose.

options.label: D
options.text: The skin and the tongue.

items.explanation: Wait, the prompt says they cannot see it. Let's re-evaluate: The student is using the skin for texture and temperature. Since the question asks which organs are working to provide 'this' information (texture/temp), and they are in the dark, the eyes are NOT providing info. Let's refine the options. Actually, the skin provides both. However, if we look at the prompt's logic, the student is using the skin. Let's correct the logic: The student uses the skin for texture and temperature. If the question asks which organ is responsible for texture/temp, it is the skin. To make it a hard question: 'Which sense is being used to detect the physical properties of the ball?'

rubric.correct: The student identifies the skin as the organ for touch/temperature.
common_misconceptions: Confusing touch with sight because they both provide information about objects.

items.concept_title: Human body parts and the senses
items.prompt: During a science experiment, a student notices that when they pinch their skin very lightly, they feel nothing, but when they pinch harder, it hurts. What does this tell us about our sense of touch?
items.helper_text: Does the skin act like one single sensor, or many different sensors?

options.label: A
options.text: Our skin only has receptors for pain, not light touch.

options.label: B
options.text: The skin has different types of receptors for different levels of pressure and pain.

options.label: C
options.text: The brain only processes information when the stimulus is very strong.

options.label: D
options.text: Touch is controlled by the eyes, not the skin.

items.explanation: The skin contains specialized sensory receptors: some detect light pressure/touch, while others (nociceptors) detect pain.

rubric.correct: The student recognizes the specialization of sensory receptors in the skin.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the skin is just one single type of sensor.
Thinking the brain ignores weak signals entirely.

items.concept_title: Human body parts and the senses
items.prompt: If a person's auditory nerve was damaged but their eardrum was perfectly healthy, what would most likely happen?
items.helper_text: Think of the nerve as a telephone wire connecting the ear to the brain.

options.label: A
options.text: They would hear very loudly because the eardrum is strong.

options.label: B
options.text: They would be able to hear sounds, but the sounds would be very quiet.

options.label: C
options.text: They would not be able to hear sounds because the signal cannot reach the brain.

options.label: D
options.text: They would start seeing sounds instead of hearing them.

items.explanation: The eardrum captures sound waves, but the nerve is the 'bridge' that carries the electrical signal to the brain. If the bridge is broken, the brain receives no information.

rubric.correct: The student understands that the nerve is essential for transmitting information to the brain.
common_misconceptions: Assuming a healthy eardrum guarantees hearing.
Thinking the eardrum is the final step in hearing.

items.concept_title: Human body parts and the senses
items.prompt: An athlete is running a race. They can feel their heart beating fast and their breath coming heavily. Which of these is a correct way to describe how their body is using its senses and internal awareness?
items.helper_text: Are the sensations coming from the outside world or from inside the body?

options.label: A
options.text: The athlete is using external senses to feel the wind.

options.label: B
options.text: The athlete is using internal awareness to sense changes inside their body.

options.label: C
options.text: The athlete is using sight to monitor their heart rate.

options.label: D
options.text: The athlete is using the sense of smell to regulate breathing.

items.explanation: While we usually think of the five senses (external), the body also has 'interoception' or internal awareness, allowing us to sense things like heartbeat and breathing.

rubric.correct: The student distinguishes between external environmental senses and internal bodily sensations.
common_misconceptions: Thinking all 'sensing' must come from the five external senses.
Confusing internal physical changes with external stimuli.

items.prompt: Siti is playing with several objects. She has a wooden block, a plastic ball, and a metal spoon. If Siti wants to find an object that is hard and does not change its shape easily when she presses it, which object should she choose?
items.helper_text: Think about which object feels the most solid and resists being squeezed.

options.label: A
options.text: The plastic ball

options.label: B
options.text: The wooden block

options.label: C
options.text: A piece of sponge

options.label: D
options.text: A balloon

items.explanation: A wooden block is a solid object that is hard and maintains its shape even when pressure is applied. A plastic ball might be hollow/squishy, a sponge is soft, and a balloon is flexible.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the wooden block as a hard, rigid object.
common_misconceptions: Confusing 'hard' with 'round' shapes.
Choosing objects that are hollow like a ball.

items.prompt: Budi is looking for an object to help him dry a wet table after cleaning. He needs an object that can absorb water. Which of these objects has the property of being absorbent?
items.helper_text: Which material is best at soaking up spilled water?

options.label: A
options.text: A glass plate

options.label: B
options.text: A plastic ruler

options.label: C
options.text: A cotton cloth

options.label: D
options.text: A metal coin

items.explanation: Absorbent objects are those that can soak up liquid. Cotton cloth is porous and can hold water, whereas glass, plastic, and metal are waterproof (non-absorbent).

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies cotton as an absorbent material.
common_misconceptions: Thinking smooth surfaces like glass are good for drying.
Confusing 'hard' objects with 'absorbent' objects.

items.prompt: Rani wants to build a small tower that can stand tall without falling over easily. She needs objects that are heavy and stable. Which group of objects is most suitable for her tower?
items.helper_text: Think about which materials are solid and heavy enough to stay in place.

options.label: A
options.text: Feathers, paper, and leaves

options.label: B
options.text: Rocks, bricks, and wooden blocks

options.label: C
options.text: Bubbles, air, and cotton candy

options.label: D
options.text: Water, juice, and milk

items.explanation: To build a stable tower, Rani needs solid objects with weight (mass) and rigidity. Rocks, bricks, and wooden blocks are solid and heavy enough to provide a stable base.

rubric.correct: The student correctly selects the group of solid, heavy objects.
common_misconceptions: Selecting lightweight objects that would blow away.
Selecting liquids which cannot hold a shape for a tower.

items.prompt: Sarah is building a small model house. She needs a material for the roof that will prevent water from entering the house and will not break easily when hit by heavy rain. Which combination of properties should she look for?
items.helper_text: Think about what happens to a sponge versus a plastic sheet when water hits them.

options.label: A
options.text: Absorbent and fragile

options.label: B
options.text: Waterproof and durable

options.label: C
options.text: Transparent and soft

options.label: D
options.text: Flexible and porous

items.explanation: To prevent water from entering, the material must be waterproof (repels water). To ensure it doesn't break easily, it must be durable (strong/long-lasting).

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies that 'waterproof' stops water and 'durable' prevents breaking.
common_misconceptions: Confusing 'absorbent' with 'waterproof'.
Thinking 'flexible' means 'strong'.

items.prompt: A chef is designing a new cooking spoon. He wants the spoon to be able to stir hot soup without burning his hand and without melting in the hot liquid. Which material property is most important for the handle?
items.helper_text: Focus on how heat moves from the soup to the hand.

options.label: A
options.text: Conductivity of heat

options.label: B
options.text: Transparency

options.label: C
options.text: Magnetism

options.label: D
options.text: Elasticity

items.explanation: The ability of a material to allow heat to pass through it is called thermal conductivity. A good handle should be a poor conductor (insulator) so heat doesn't travel to the hand.

rubric.correct: The student connects the sensation of heat transfer to the property of conductivity.
common_misconceptions: Choosing 'elasticity' because the spoon might bend.
Choosing 'transparency' because it looks nice.

items.prompt: You have three mystery objects: Object X is hard and shiny; Object Y is soft and can be stretched; Object Z is clear and allows light to pass through perfectly. If you wanted to make a window for a birdcage, which object would be the best choice and why?
items.helper_text: What is the main purpose of a window?

options.label: A
options.text: Object X, because it is hard and won't break.

options.label: B
options.text: Object Y, because it is stretchy and flexible.

options.label: C
options.text: Object Z, because it is transparent and lets light in.

options.label: D
options.text: Object X, because it is shiny and reflects light.

items.explanation: A window's primary function is to allow light to pass through so animals can see. 'Transparent' is the specific property of Object Z that allows this.

rubric.correct: The student identifies the relationship between transparency and the function of a window.
common_misconceptions: Choosing Object X because they think 'hard' is more important than 'seeing through'.

items.prompt: An engineer is choosing a material for a new playground slide. The slide must be smooth so children slide down easily, but it must also be strong enough to hold the weight of many children without bending. Which pair of properties is required?
items.helper_text: Think about how friction affects sliding and how weight affects shape.

options.label: A
options.text: Rough and flexible

options.label: B
options.text: Smooth and rigid

options.label: C
options.text: Soft and transparent

options.label: D
options.text: Rough and hard

items.explanation: 'Smooth' reduces friction for easy sliding, and 'rigid' (the opposite of flexible) ensures the structure holds its shape under weight.

rubric.correct: The student correctly matches 'smooth' to movement and 'rigid' to structural strength.
common_misconceptions: Confusing 'rigid' with 'hard' (though similar, rigidity specifically refers to resisting bending).

items.prompt: If you drop a glass marble and a rubber ball on a hard floor, the marble bounces very little, while the rubber ball bounces very high. What does this tell you about the difference in their properties?
items.helper_text: Which object 'springs back' better?

options.label: A
options.text: The marble is more elastic than the rubber ball.

options.label: B
options.text: The rubber ball has more elasticity than the marble.

options.label: C
options.text: The marble is more transparent than the rubber ball.

options.label: D
options.text: The rubber ball is more rigid than the marble.

items.explanation: Elasticity is the ability of an object to return to its original shape after being compressed. A high bounce indicates high elasticity.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies elasticity as the cause of the bouncing behavior.
common_misconceptions: Thinking 'harder' objects always bounce higher.

items.prompt: A scientist is testing a new material for a raincoat. She finds that when she pours water on it, the water beads up and rolls off, but the material is very heavy and hard to fold. Which statement is true?
items.helper_text: Look at the two specific behaviors: water behavior and folding behavior.

options.label: A
options.text: The material is waterproof but not flexible.

options.label: B
options.text: The material is absorbent and rigid.

options.label: C
options.text: The material is transparent and soft.

options.label: D
options.text: The material is flexible but not waterproof.

items.explanation: Water rolling off means it is waterproof. Being 'hard to fold' means it lacks flexibility.

rubric.correct: The student correctly maps the observations to the scientific terms 'waterproof' and 'flexible'.
common_misconceptions: Thinking 'beading water' means the material is 'absorbent'.

items.prompt: Compare a piece of steel and a piece of sponge. If you apply the same amount of pressure (pushing force) to both, why does the sponge change shape while the steel does not?
items.helper_text: Think about which object is easier to squish.

options.label: A
options.text: The steel is more absorbent than the sponge.

options.label: B
options.text: The sponge is more elastic/flexible than the steel.

options.label: C
options.text: The steel is more transparent than the sponge.

options.label: D
options.text: The sponge is more rigid than the steel.

items.explanation: The ability to change shape under pressure and return (or simply change) is related to flexibility and elasticity. Steel is rigid and resists changing shape.

rubric.correct: The student identifies that the difference in shape-changing ability is due to flexibility/elasticity.
common_misconceptions: Confusing 'hardness' with 'rigidity'.

items.concept_title: Earth, moon, sun, and the solar system
items.prompt: During a science experiment, Sarah observes that the Moon appears to change its shape in the night sky over several weeks. Which of the following best explains why the Moon's visible shape changes?
items.helper_text: Think about the Moon's movement around the Earth and how much sunlight hits the side facing us.

options.label: A
options.text: The Earth casts a shadow on the Moon, blocking the sunlight.

options.label: B
options.text: The Moon moves around the Earth, changing how much of its lit side we can see.

options.label: C
options.text: Clouds in the atmosphere cover different parts of the Moon each night.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun's light gets weaker as the Moon moves further away from the Earth.

items.explanation: The Moon does not produce its own light; it reflects sunlight. As the Moon orbits the Earth, our view of the half of the Moon that is illuminated by the Sun changes, creating the different phases (like crescent, half, or full).

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies that the Moon's phases are caused by its orbit around Earth changing our perspective of its illuminated half.
common_misconceptions: Thinking that lunar phases are caused by Earth's shadow (which is actually a lunar eclipse).
Thinking that the Moon itself changes shape physically.

items.concept_title: Earth, moon, sun, and the solar system
items.prompt: During a solar eclipse, the Moon passes directly between the Earth and the Sun. If the Moon's orbit were perfectly flat and aligned with the Earth's orbit around the Sun at all times, how would the frequency of solar eclipses change?
items.helper_text: Think about what happens during a New Moon if the Moon is always in the same plane as the Earth and Sun.

options.label: A
options.text: Solar eclipses would happen every single month.

options.label: B
options.text: Solar eclipses would never happen because the Sun is too large.

options.label: C
options.text: Solar eclipses would only happen during the summer season.

options.label: D
options.text: Solar eclipses would happen only when the Moon is at its furthest point from Earth.

items.explanation: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon blocks the Sun's light. Currently, eclipses are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted. If the orbit were perfectly aligned (flat), every New Moon phase would result in the Moon passing directly in front of the Sun.

rubric.correct: The student understands that the tilt of the Moon's orbit is the reason eclipses are not monthly events.
common_misconceptions: Thinking eclipses are caused by the distance of the Moon rather than its orbital alignment.
Believing the Sun's size prevents eclipses regardless of alignment.

items.concept_title: Earth, moon, sun, and the solar system
items.prompt: An astronaut on a planet is observing the Sun. This planet takes 365 days to orbit its star, and the planet rotates on its axis once every 24 hours. If the planet suddenly stopped rotating on its axis but continued to orbit the star, what would happen to the concept of 'days' on that planet?
items.helper_text: Distinguish between rotation (spinning) and revolution (orbiting).

options.label: A
options.text: There would be no days or nights at all.

options.label: B
options.text: One 'day' (one full cycle of light and dark) would last exactly one year.

options.label: C
options.text: One 'day' would last exactly 24 hours, but the direction would change.

options.label: D
options.text: The planet would have many days per year because of the orbital motion.

items.explanation: A day is defined by the cycle of light and dark. If a planet does not rotate on its axis, its position relative to the Sun only changes as it moves around the star. It would take one full revolution (one year) for the same side of the planet to face the Sun again.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies that orbital revolution alone creates a day-night cycle if rotation is zero.
common_misconceptions: Confusing rotation with revolution.
Assuming light and dark are permanent based on which side faces the Sun initially.

items.concept_title: Earth, moon, sun, and the solar system
items.prompt: If Earth were moved to a position much closer to the Sun, while keeping its current speed and tilt, how would the length of a year and the seasons be affected?
items.helper_text: Consider how distance affects both orbital speed and heat intensity.

options.label: A
options.text: The year would be longer and seasons would disappear.

options.label: B
options.text: The year would be shorter and seasons would become more extreme.

options.label: C
options.text: The year would be shorter and seasons would become milder.

options.label: D
options.text: The year would be longer and seasons would become more extreme.

items.explanation: According to Kepler's laws, a closer orbit requires a higher orbital velocity and a shorter path, resulting in a shorter year. Being closer to the Sun increases the intensity of solar radiation, making the temperature changes caused by the tilt (seasons) much more extreme.

rubric.correct: The student connects orbital distance to both orbital period and solar intensity.
common_misconceptions: Thinking a closer orbit means a slower path.
Thinking seasons are caused by distance rather than tilt.

items.concept_title: Earth, moon, sun, and the solar system
items.prompt: A student observes that the Moon appears to change shape over several weeks. Which of the following best explains why we see different phases of the Moon instead of seeing the whole Moon all the time?
items.helper_text: Remember that the Moon does not produce its own light; it reflects the Sun.

options.label: A
options.text: The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, blocking its light.

options.label: B
options.text: The Moon is reflecting different amounts of sunlight based on its position relative to Earth and the Sun.

options.label: C
options.text: Clouds in Earth's atmosphere block different parts of the Moon.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon itself is changing its physical shape due to gravity.

items.explanation: Moon phases are caused by the Moon's orbit around Earth. As it moves, we see different portions of its illuminated half (the half lit by the Sun) from our perspective on Earth.

rubric.correct: The student identifies the relative positions of the Sun, Moon, and Earth as the cause of phases.
common_misconceptions: Confusing lunar phases with lunar eclipses (Earth's shadow).
Thinking the Moon actually changes shape.

items.concept_title: Earth, moon, sun, and the solar system
items.prompt: Imagine a new planet is discovered in our solar system. It is located between Mars and Jupiter. Which of the following is most likely true about this planet?
items.helper_text: Recall the order of the planets and the location of the gas giants.

options.label: A
options.text: It is a gas giant and is much larger than Earth.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a terrestrial planet with a rocky surface.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a dwarf planet located in the Kuiper Belt.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a star that provides light to the inner planets.

items.explanation: The region between Mars and Jupiter is the Asteroid Belt, which leads into the outer solar system dominated by Gas Giants (Jupiter, Saturn, etc.). A planet in this region would likely be a gas giant or a large object formed in that zone.

rubric.correct: The student uses the solar system model to predict the characteristics of a planet based on its location.
common_misconceptions: Assuming all planets in the solar system are rocky.
Confusing the asteroid belt location with the Kuiper belt.

items.concept_title: Earth, moon, sun, and the solar system
items.prompt: If the Earth's axis were not tilted and was perfectly upright relative to its orbit around the Sun, what would be the most significant impact on Earth's climate?
items.helper_text: What causes the difference in sunlight intensity between summer and winter?

options.label: A
options.text: The Earth would experience much hotter summers.

options.label: B
options.text: The Earth would have no seasons at all.

options.label: C
options.text: The Earth would experience constant day and night for 6 months.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun would appear to move across the sky faster.

items.explanation: Seasons are caused by the Earth's axial tilt, which changes the angle of sunlight and the length of days at different latitudes throughout the year. If the axis were upright, the sunlight hitting any given latitude would remain constant throughout the orbit, eliminating seasonal changes.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the axial tilt as the primary cause of seasonal variation.
common_misconceptions: Thinking seasons are caused by the distance from the Sun.
Thinking the tilt causes the day/night cycle (which is caused by rotation).

items.concept_title: Earth, moon, sun, and the solar system
items.prompt: Why does the Sun appear to 'rise' in the East and 'set' in the West every day?
items.helper_text: Is the Sun actually moving around us, or are we spinning?

options.label: A
options.text: Because the Sun is traveling in a circle around the Earth.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the Earth rotates on its axis from West to East.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the Earth orbits the Sun from East to West.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the Sun moves slightly every day due to its own rotation.

items.explanation: The apparent motion of the Sun is a result of Earth's rotation. Because Earth spins toward the East (counter-clockwise when viewed from the North Pole), objects in the sky appear to move in the opposite direction (Westward).

rubric.correct: The student distinguishes between apparent motion and actual motion caused by rotation.
common_misconceptions: Believing in the geocentric model (Sun moving around Earth).
Confusing rotation with revolution.

items.prompt: Siti is playing in a room with a very large window. She notices that when she holds a clear glass of water in front of a bright flashlight, a bright spot of light appears on the wall behind it. However, when she places a thick wooden book in front of the flashlight, no light reaches the wall, and a dark shape is formed. What is the main reason for this difference?
items.helper_text: Think about whether light can pass through the object or if it gets stopped by it.

options.label: A
options.text: The glass is transparent and allows light to pass through, while the book is opaque and blocks light.

options.label: B
options.text: The glass is harder than the book, so light travels faster through it.

options.label: C
options.text: The light from the flashlight is too weak to pass through the wooden book.

options.label: D
options.text: The book absorbs all the sound in the room, preventing the light from moving.

items.explanation: Light interacts differently with materials based on their properties. Transparent materials like clear glass allow light to pass through them easily. Opaque materials like wood block light from passing through, which creates a shadow.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies that the difference is caused by the transparency of the glass versus the opacity of the book.
common_misconceptions: Thinking that the speed of light changes based on the hardness of the object.
Confusing the properties of light with the properties of sound.

items.prompt: Sarah is standing in a dark room with a flashlight. She points the flashlight at a clear glass window, then at a wooden door, and finally at a shiny silver mirror. In which order will she observe the light being reflected, transmitted, and absorbed/blocked?
items.helper_text: Think about how different materials interact with light rays.

options.label: A
options.text: Mirror (Reflected), Window (Transmitted), Door (Absorbed/Blocked)

options.label: B
options.text: Window (Transmitted), Mirror (Reflected), Door (Absorbed/Blocked)

options.label: C
options.text: Door (Absorbed/Blocked), Window (Transmitted), Mirror (Reflected)

options.label: D
options.text: Mirror (Reflected), Door (Absorbed/Blocked), Window (Transmitted)

items.explanation: A mirror reflects light to create an image, a clear glass window allows light to pass through (transmission), and a wooden door is opaque, meaning it absorbs or blocks the light.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the unique interaction of light with transparent, translucent, and opaque objects.
common_misconceptions: Confusing transmission with reflection.
Assuming all solid objects block light in the same way.

items.prompt: An astronaut is exploring the moon where there is no atmosphere. If the astronaut drops a heavy metal hammer and a light feather at the same time, and then shouts loudly, what will happen regarding light and sound?
items.helper_text: Remember that sound needs a medium to travel, but light does not.

options.label: A
options.text: Both fall at different speeds, and the shout can be heard clearly.

options.label: B
options.text: Both fall at the same speed, and the shout can be heard clearly.

options.label: C
options.text: Both fall at the same speed, but the shout cannot be heard.

options.label: D
options.text: Both fall at different speeds, and the shout cannot be heard.

items.explanation: In a vacuum (no atmosphere), there is no air resistance to slow the feather, so they fall at the same rate. However, sound requires a medium (like air) to travel; without air, sound cannot propagate.

rubric.correct: The student connects the absence of a medium to the inability of sound to travel.
common_misconceptions: Thinking sound can travel through a vacuum.
Thinking air resistance still affects objects in a vacuum.

items.prompt: A student places a pencil in a half-filled glass of water. When looking from the side, the pencil appears broken or bent at the water's surface. Why does this phenomenon occur?
items.helper_text: Think about what happens to light when it changes speed in different materials.

options.label: A
options.text: The water acts as a mirror and reflects the image of the pencil.

options.label: B
options.text: The light bends as it moves from the air into the denser water medium.

options.label: C
options.text: The water absorbs the light rays, making the bottom part of the pencil invisible.

options.label: D
options.text: The glass lens magnifies the pencil, making it look larger and shifted.

items.explanation: This is refraction. Light changes speed when it moves from one medium (air) to another (water), causing the light rays to bend, which makes the object appear displaced.

rubric.correct: The student identifies refraction as the cause of light bending between media.
common_misconceptions: Thinking it is a reflection problem.
Thinking the water is simply 'hiding' part of the pencil.

items.prompt: If you are in a very noisy classroom and you close your ears tightly with your hands, you can still feel the vibrations of a loud drum nearby. Which sense and property are being demonstrated?
items.helper_text: Focus on which sense is being used to perceive the 'noise' when the ears are blocked.

options.label: A
options.text: Hearing and the ability of sound to travel through solids.

options.label: B
options.text: Sight and the ability of light to travel through objects.

options.label: C
options.text: Touch and the ability of sound to travel through solids.

options.label: D
options.text: Touch and the ability of light to travel through air.

items.explanation: By closing the ears, the student is using the sense of touch (feeling vibrations). Sound travels as mechanical waves that can move through air and solids, causing physical vibrations.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies that vibrations can be felt via touch and that sound travels through media.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the sense of hearing with the physical sensation of vibration.
Thinking sound only travels through air.

items.prompt: A person is standing in a dark room with their eyes closed. They smell freshly baked bread and hear a bell ringing. Which statement best describes their sensory experience?
items.helper_text: Match the stimulus (bread/bell) to the organ used to detect it.

options.label: A
options.text: They are using sight and sound to navigate the room.

options.label: B
options.text: They are using smell and hearing to perceive their environment.

options.label: C
options.text: They are using touch and smell to perceive the bread.

options.label: D
options.text: They are using sight and smell to identify the bell.

items.explanation: The eyes are closed (no sight), the smell of bread is detected by the nose (smell), and the bell is detected by the ears (hearing).

rubric.correct: The student correctly matches the environmental stimuli to the active senses.
common_misconceptions: Assuming sight is always the primary sense used in descriptions.
Misidentifying the organ used for smell.

items.prompt: A scientist is testing how sound travels. They use three different materials: a wooden plank, a metal rod, and a plastic string. If they tap one end of each, which material will likely allow the sound to travel the fastest and most clearly due to its particle arrangement?
items.helper_text: Think about how closely the tiny particles are packed in different solids.

options.label: A
options.text: The plastic string, because it is flexible.

options.label: B
options.text: The wooden plank, because it is thick.

options.label: C
options.text: The metal rod, because its particles are tightly packed and elastic.

options.label: D
options.text: All three will travel at the same speed because they are all solids.

items.explanation: Sound travels fastest through solids where particles are closely packed. Metals are particularly good conductors of sound because their atoms are tightly arranged and can pass vibrations very efficiently.

rubric.correct: The student understands that particle density and material type affect sound conduction.
common_misconceptions: Thinking sound travels at the same speed in all solids.
Thinking flexibility (plastic) helps sound travel faster.

items.prompt: During a solar eclipse, the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun. Why does the sky become dark even though the Sun is still shining?
items.helper_text: Consider the concept of 'opaque' and how light travels in straight lines.

options.label: A
options.text: The Moon absorbs all the light from the Sun and turns it into heat.

options.label: B
options.text: The Moon reflects the sunlight back into space, away from Earth.

options.label: C
options.text: The Moon acts as an opaque object that blocks the light path to Earth.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun stops producing light temporarily during an eclipse.

items.explanation: The Moon is an opaque object. During an eclipse, it is positioned in a way that it blocks the straight-line path of light rays from the Sun to the Earth, creating a shadow.

rubric.correct: The student correctly applies the concept of opacity and light traveling in straight lines to a natural phenomenon.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the Sun actually turns off.
Confusing blocking light (opacity) with absorbing light.

items.concept_title: Earth's surface features and natural resources
items.prompt: A village is located at the foot of a large, sloping mountain. The villagers want to plant crops that can grow well in fertile soil and help prevent landslides. Which type of land feature and resource management would be most suitable for them?
items.helper_text: Think about how to stop soil from sliding down a hill when it rains.

options.label: A
options.text: Planting crops in a flat desert area to save water.

options.label: B
options.text: Building houses on a steep cliff to see the view.

options.label: C
options.text: Creating terrace farming on the mountain slopes to hold the soil.

options.label: D
options.text: Digging deep mines in the middle of the village forest.

items.explanation: Terrace farming (making steps on a slope) is a direct application of managing mountain land features. It helps slow down water runoff and keeps the fertile soil in place, preventing landslides.

rubric.correct: The student identifies that terracing is a way to adapt farming to mountainous terrain.
common_misconceptions: Thinking that flat land is always the best for all types of farming.
Confusing land features with mineral resources like mining.

items.concept_title: Earth's surface features and natural resources
items.prompt: If a large forest is cleared completely to build a massive shopping mall, what is the most likely impact on the natural resources of that area?
items.helper_text: Consider what happens to rainwater when there are no tree roots to soak it up.

options.label: A
options.text: The air quality will improve because there is more space for cars.

options.label: B
options.text: The water cycle might be disrupted, potentially leading to floods.

options.label: C
options.text: The soil will become more fertile because the trees are gone.

options.label: D
options.text: The local animals will find new homes inside the shopping mall.

items.explanation: Forests play a crucial role in the water cycle by absorbing rainwater. Removing them reduces the ground's ability to soak up water, which increases surface runoff and the risk of flooding.

rubric.correct: The student understands the connection between forest cover and water management.
common_misconceptions: Believing that removing vegetation has no effect on water flow.
Assuming that human buildings can replace the ecological functions of a forest.

items.concept_title: Earth's surface features and natural resources
items.prompt: A village is located at the foot of a steep mountain with very thin soil and heavy rainfall. The villagers want to start a farm to improve their economy. Which combination of land use and natural resource management would be most effective to prevent landslides while still producing crops?
items.helper_text: Think about how plants and land shapes can stop soil from sliding down during rain.

options.label: A
options.text: Planting large corn fields across the entire slope to maximize harvest.

options.label: B
options.text: Building concrete walls around the village and planting only decorative flowers.

options.label: C
options.text: Using terrace farming and planting deep-rooted trees to hold the soil.

options.label: D
options.text: Digging deep irrigation canals to move water away from the mountain quickly.

items.explanation: Terrace farming reduces the speed of water runoff on steep slopes, and deep-rooted trees act as natural anchors for the soil, preventing erosion and landslides in high-rainfall areas.

rubric.correct: The student identifies that terracing and root systems work together to stabilize slopes.
common_misconceptions: Assuming more crops always means better farming regardless of terrain.
Thinking that moving water quickly through canals is always safer than slowing it down.

items.concept_title: Earth's surface features and natural resources
items.prompt: An island has a lot of volcanic soil and is surrounded by shallow, warm seas. If a community wants to develop a sustainable economy that uses both land and sea resources, which plan is most balanced?
items.helper_text: Look for the option that uses the natural gifts of the island without damaging them.

options.label: A
options.text: Building large factories to process minerals found in the volcanic rocks.

options.label: B
options.text: Developing organic vegetable farming and coral reef-based eco-tourism.

options.label: C
options.text: Using all the land for housing to accommodate more tourists.

options.label: D
options.text: Dredging the shallow sea to create deep ports for large cargo ships.

items.explanation: Volcanic soil is highly fertile for organic farming, and shallow warm seas are ideal for coral reefs. This plan uses the natural advantages of the environment without destroying them.

rubric.correct: The student connects volcanic soil fertility and marine biodiversity to sustainable activities.
common_misconceptions: Focusing only on industrial growth (minerals) without considering environmental impact.
Ignoring the biological value of the shallow sea.

items.concept_title: Earth's surface features and natural resources
items.prompt: If a large forest is cleared to create a massive cattle ranch, what is the most likely long-term impact on the local water cycle and soil quality?
items.helper_text: Consider what happens to the rain and the dirt when the 'anchors' (trees) are gone.

options.label: A
options.text: The soil will become richer due to animal waste, and rainfall will increase.

options.label: B
options.text: The water cycle will speed up, and the soil will become more stable.

options.label: C
options.text: The soil will lose nutrients and erode easily, and the area may experience less rainfall.

options.label: D
options.text: The groundwater levels will rise because there are fewer trees to drink the water.

items.explanation: Trees play a crucial role in transpiration (releasing moisture into the air) and holding soil together. Removing them leads to less moisture in the air and higher rates of soil erosion.

rubric.correct: The student understands the link between vegetation, transpiration, and soil stability.
common_misconceptions: Thinking animal waste alone can replace the complex ecosystem of a forest.
Assuming less water consumption by trees means more water is available for everything else.

items.concept_title: Earth's surface features and natural resources
items.prompt: A coastal town experiences frequent flooding during high tides. The town council is debating whether to build a giant sea wall or to restore the nearby mangrove forests. Which approach is better for long-term natural resource protection?
items.helper_text: Compare a man-made structure with a biological solution.

options.label: A
options.text: The sea wall, because it provides a permanent and unbreakable barrier.

options.label: B
options.text: The mangrove forest, because it acts as a natural buffer and provides habitats.

options.label: C
options.text: The sea wall, because it allows more sunlight to reach the ocean floor.

options.label: D
options.text: The mangrove forest, because it will stop all waves from ever reaching the land.

items.explanation: Mangroves are natural buffers that absorb wave energy and prevent erosion, while also serving as nurseries for fish, thus protecting marine resources.

rubric.correct: The student recognizes the multi-functional benefits of mangroves over static man-made walls.
common_misconceptions: Believing man-made structures are always more effective than nature.
Thinking mangroves completely stop all water movement rather than absorbing energy.

items.concept_title: Earth's surface features and natural resources
items.prompt: In a region with high plateau land and very little river activity, which natural resource would be most difficult to utilize for large-scale agriculture without significant technology?
items.helper_text: What is the one thing every plant absolutely needs to grow in a field?

options.label: A
options.text: Sunlight for solar energy.

options.label: B
options.text: Wind for wind turbines.

options.label: C
options.text: Fresh water for irrigation.

options.label: D
options.text: Space for building greenhouses.

items.explanation: Agriculture requires water. In a plateau with little river activity, water is scarce, making irrigation difficult without advanced technology like deep wells or long-distance pipelines.

rubric.correct: The student identifies water scarcity as the primary limiting factor in the described geography.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the difficulty of building on high land with the difficulty of finding water.
Thinking sunlight or wind are harder to access on a plateau.

items.concept_title: Earth's surface features and natural resources
items.prompt: A mining company wants to extract coal from a mountain range. After the mining is finished, the land is left as a large, deep hole. What is the most effective way to restore this land feature to be useful again?
items.helper_text: How can we turn a damaged area back into a healthy part of nature?

options.label: A
options.text: Filling the hole with more coal to keep the mountain shape.

options.label: B
options.text: Covering the area with plastic sheets to prevent rain from entering.

options.label: C
options.text: Refilling the area with soil and planting native vegetation to create a park or forest.

options.label: D
options.text: Leaving it as a deep lake to provide water for the nearby city.

items.explanation: Land reclamation involves restoring the land to a functional state, such as a forest or park, which helps stabilize the soil and restores local biodiversity.

rubric.correct: The student understands the concept of land reclamation and ecological restoration.
common_misconceptions: Thinking a deep hole is automatically a good way to make a lake (it may be toxic/unstable).
Assuming the land can simply be 'left alone' to fix itself without help.

items.concept_title: Earth's surface features and natural resources
items.prompt: Compare a river delta to a mountain peak. Which statement correctly analyzes the relationship between their surface features and the natural resources they typically provide?
items.helper_text: Think about what a river carries down from the mountains to the sea.

options.label: A
options.text: Both provide high amounts of mineral resources like gold and diamonds.

options.label: B
options.text: Mountain peaks are better for fishing, while deltas are better for mining.

options.label: C
options.text: Deltas provide fertile silt for farming, while mountains provide gravity for water flow.

options.label: D
options.text: Deltas are formed by wind, while mountains are formed by water deposition.

items.explanation: Rivers carry sediment (silt) and deposit it at deltas, creating fertile land. Mountains provide the elevation needed for rivers to flow downward via gravity.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the geological processes and resulting resources of both features.
common_misconceptions: Confusing deposition (deltas) with erosion (mountains).
Incorrectly assigning mineral/fishing resources to the wrong landforms.

items.prompt: Siti is helping her mother in the kitchen. She accidentally dropped a spoonful of salt into a bowl of sand. Which method should Siti use to separate the salt from the sand so she can get the salt back?
items.helper_text: Think about which substance will disappear into the water and which will stay solid.

options.label: A
options.text: Using a sieve to catch the salt

options.label: B
options.text: Adding water, stirring, and then evaporating the water

options.label: C
options.text: Using a magnet to pull the salt out

options.label: D
options.text: Picking the salt out with her hands

items.explanation: Salt dissolves in water while sand does not. By adding water, the salt forms a solution. The sand can then be filtered out, and the remaining saltwater can be heated (evaporation) to leave the salt crystals behind.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies that a multi-step process involving solubility and evaporation is needed.
common_misconceptions: Thinking that a sieve can separate tiny salt grains from sand.
Thinking that magnetism can attract salt.

items.prompt: A construction worker has a mixture of large stones, fine sand, and water in a bucket. He needs to collect only the fine sand to use for making cement. What is the most effective way to separate the sand from the stones and water?
items.helper_text: Consider which tool works best when objects are different sizes.

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporating the water to leave the sand and stones

options.label: B
options.text: Using a magnet to pull the sand out

options.label: C
options.text: Using a sieve to filter out the large stones

options.label: D
options.text: Letting the mixture sit until the sand turns into gas

items.explanation: A sieve (or strainer) is used to separate mixtures based on particle size. The holes in the sieve will allow the water and fine sand to pass through, while the large stones will be caught on top.

rubric.correct: The student correctly applies the concept of filtration/sieving based on particle size.
common_misconceptions: Assuming evaporation is the fastest way to get sand.
Confusing the properties of sand with magnetic materials.

items.prompt: A scientist accidentally mixed fine iron filings, coarse sand, and small salt crystals in a beaker. Which sequence of methods should the scientist use to recover all three substances in their original form?
items.helper_text: Think about the order: you must remove the magnetic part before adding water, otherwise the iron will be hard to pick out.

options.label: A
options.text: Filtration $\rightarrow$ Evaporation $\rightarrow$ Magnetism

options.label: B
options.text: Magnetism $\rightarrow$ Dissolving in water $\rightarrow$ Filtration $\rightarrow$ Evaporation

options.label: C
options.text: Evaporation $\rightarrow$ Magnetism $\rightarrow$ Filtration

options.label: D
options.text: Dissolving in water $\rightarrow$ Magnetism $\rightarrow$ Evaporation

items.explanation: First, use a magnet to remove the iron filings. Second, add water to dissolve the salt, leaving the sand undissolved. Third, use filtration to separate the sand from the saltwater. Finally, use evaporation to recover the salt from the water.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the multi-step logical progression of separation.
common_misconceptions: Thinking magnetism can be done after adding water.
Forgetting that salt needs water to be separated from sand via filtration.

items.prompt: In a coastal village, people use a large basin of seawater to collect salt. They leave the water in the sun for several days until the salt remains at the bottom. Which principle is being applied here, and what happens to the water?
items.helper_text: Focus on what happens to the liquid part when it is exposed to heat.

options.label: A
options.text: Filtration; the water is trapped by the salt crystals.

options.label: B
options.text: Decantation; the water turns into a solid.

options.label: C
options.text: Evaporation; the water changes from liquid to gas.

options.label: D
options.text: Sieving; the water passes through the salt particles.

items.explanation: The sun provides heat energy that causes the liquid water to evaporate into water vapor (gas), leaving the solid salt behind.

rubric.correct: The student links the environmental process to the scientific concept of evaporation.
common_misconceptions: Confusing evaporation with decantation.
Thinking the water disappears into nothingness rather than changing state.

items.prompt: You are given a mixture of muddy water and large pebbles. You want to get clear water and the pebbles back. If you use a filter paper, what will be the result?
items.helper_text: Remember that filtration separates solids from liquids based on particle size.

options.label: A
options.text: The pebbles and mud will stay on the paper, and clear water will pass through.

options.label: B
options.text: The pebbles will stay on the paper, while the mud and water pass through.

options.label: C
options.text: The pebbles and water will pass through, while the mud stays on the paper.

options.label: D
options.text: Everything will pass through the paper, but the water will become clear.

items.explanation: Filter paper has tiny pores that allow liquid (water) to pass through but trap solid particles (mud and pebbles) that are larger than the pores.

rubric.correct: The student correctly predicts the outcome of a filtration process.
common_misconceptions: Assuming the mud is small enough to pass through the filter.
Thinking the pebbles are too large to be caught by a filter.

items.prompt: A chef accidentally dropped a box of dried peppercorns into a bowl of fine white flour. Which method would be the most efficient way to separate the peppercorns from the flour without using water?
items.helper_text: Think about which substance is larger and which one should pass through the holes.

options.label: A
options.text: Dissolving the mixture in water.

options.label: B
options.text: Using a magnet to pull out the peppercorns.

options.label: C
options.text: Using a sieve with holes larger than the peppercorns.

options.label: D
options.text: Using a sieve with holes smaller than the peppercorns.

items.explanation: Sieving works by passing a mixture through a mesh. If the holes are larger than the peppercorns, the peppercorns will fall through. Wait—correction: To separate peppercorns (large) from flour (small), the peppercorns should stay in the sieve if the holes are small, OR if we want to remove the flour, we use a sieve where the flour falls through. Actually, the most efficient way to separate the *peppercorns* is to use a sieve where the flour falls through the holes, leaving the peppercorns on top. Therefore, a sieve with holes smaller than the peppercorns but larger than the flour is needed. Option C is the standard application: the flour falls through, peppercorns remain.

rubric.correct: The student identifies sieving as the correct method for size-based separation.
common_misconceptions: Choosing magnetism (peppercorns are not magnetic).
Choosing dissolving (flour and peppercorns don't dissolve easily/differently enough).

items.prompt: A mixture contains oil, water, and sand. If you want to separate these three components, what is the correct logical order?
items.helper_text: First, deal with the solid. Then, deal with the two liquids that don't mix.

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporation $\rightarrow$ Magnetism $\rightarrow$ Filtration

options.label: B
options.text: Filtration (to remove sand) $\rightarrow$ Decantation (to separate oil and water)

options.label: C
options.text: Decantation (to remove sand) $\rightarrow$ Evaporation (to remove oil)

options.label: D
options.text: Sieving (to remove oil) $\rightarrow$ Filtration (to remove water)

items.explanation: First, filtration removes the solid sand. The remaining liquid is a mixture of oil and water. Since oil floats on water and they do not mix (immiscible), they can be separated by decantation (pouring off the top layer).

rubric.correct: The student understands how to handle a multi-phase mixture (solid and two immiscible liquids).
common_misconceptions: Trying to use evaporation to separate oil and water (which is difficult/dangerous).
Thinking sand can be separated by decantation easily.

items.prompt: Why is it impossible to separate salt from a saltwater solution using only a filter paper and a funnel?
items.helper_text: Think about the difference between a 'mixture of solids' and a 'solution'.

options.label: A
options.text: Because salt is a liquid and cannot be caught.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the salt particles are too large for the paper.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the salt has dissolved and become part of the liquid solution.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the filter paper will dissolve in the saltwater.

items.explanation: When salt dissolves in water, it breaks down into particles so small that they pass through the pores of the filter paper along with the water molecules. Only evaporation can separate them.

rubric.correct: The student recognizes the nature of a solution and the limitations of filtration.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the salt is still a visible solid.
Thinking the filter paper is the problem, rather than the particle size.

items.prompt: An engineer needs to clean a mixture of crushed stones and fine dust to reuse the stones for construction. Which tool and method would be most effective?
items.helper_text: Identify the physical property that differs between the stones and the dust.

options.label: A
options.text: A magnet and magnetism

options.label: B
options.text: A sieve and sieving

options.label: C
options.text: A filter paper and filtration

options.label: D
options.text: A heating tray and evaporation

items.explanation: The stones and dust are both solids, but they differ significantly in size. A sieve allows the fine dust to fall through the mesh while the larger stones stay on top.

rubric.correct: The student selects the appropriate tool based on the physical property of size.
common_misconceptions: Choosing filtration (which is for liquids).
Choosing magnetism (dust and stones are usually non-magnetic).
